heading: Pricing rules for advertised rental properties
text: Properties must be advertised at a fixed rent. Rental providers and agents cannot advertise a property with a price range, ask for or accept rent higher than the advertised amount, seek more than one month's rent in advance, advertise a property that does not meet the rental minimum standards, or charge fees to view a property. Concerns about advertised properties can be reported to Consumer Affairs Victoria.

heading: Rental application form
text: From 31 March 2026, rental providers must use the prescribed rental application form, which limits the information collected to what is needed to assess suitability and capacity to pay rent.

heading: Information that can be requested
text: Personal details (full name, date of birth, current address, phone, email); employment details (current or most recent employer, net weekly income, date employment ended); up to two financial documents from pay slips, a bank statement without transaction details, or Centrelink payment statements (or, for irregular income, employment history or proof of savings); up to two identity documents (such as a driver licence, Medicare card, passport or student ID); rental history (contact details of previous rental providers); personal references; the desired lease term and move-in date. Rental providers using tenancy databases must tell applicants which databases they use.

heading: Information that cannot be requested
text: Rental providers and agents cannot ask about history of legal action or disputes with rental providers, bond claim history, bank statements showing daily transactions (applicants can redact them), protected attributes under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 without written justification, or anything outside the prescribed application form.

heading: Choosing a renter
text: Rental providers can choose applicants based on suitability, such as rental history and capacity to pay, but discrimination based on attributes such as age, disability, race or religion is unlawful. Rental providers generally cannot refuse applicants with children under 16, except where the property is the rental provider's main residence or is unsuitable for children.

heading: Holding deposits
text: A holding deposit may be requested before the agreement is signed. It must be refunded once both parties sign the agreement, or refunded if no agreement is reached.

page_title: Bond amounts and paying a bond
heading: What is a bond?
text: A bond is a payment that rental providers (landlords) can request from renters at the start of a rental agreement (lease). It is security for the rental provider and covers potential costs when the renter moves out. The Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) holds bonds in trust. The bond is the renter's money and should be repaid to the renter in most circumstances. Rent and bond are different: a bond cannot be used to pay rent. Renters who have paid a bond receive a condition report before moving in. Eligible renters may transfer existing bond money to a new property through the Portable Rental Bond Scheme.

page_title: Bond amounts and paying a bond
heading: Maximum bond amounts
text: Generally, a bond cannot be more than one month's rent. A higher bond is only allowed if the weekly rent is more than $900, or if VCAT makes an order because of the character of the property or the quality of its furnishings. Rooming houses: the maximum bond is 28 days' rent for fixed-term agreements or 14 days' rent otherwise. Caravan parks: the bond cannot be more than one month's rent. Residential park site tenants: the maximum bond is one month's rent (where rent is $900 a week or less).

page_title: Bond amounts and paying a bond
heading: How and when bonds are paid
text: Paying a bond is not compulsory unless the rental agreement requires it. Renters may pay the rental provider, who then lodges it with the RTBA (captured text: within 14 days), pay the RTBA directly, or use the Portable Rental Bond Scheme. The RTBA issues a receipt with a bond number within 7 days of receiving the money. When several renters pay the RTBA directly, only one renter can submit the full payment, so co-renters should decide beforehand who pays and how they reimburse each other.

page_title: Bond amounts and paying a bond
heading: Homes Victoria bond loans
text: Government bond loans help people on low incomes who cannot pay a bond any other way.

page_title: Bond amounts and paying a bond
heading: Extra bond requests
text: Rental providers can only ask for additional bond in these circumstances: long-term agreements (more than 5 years, renewed for at least another 5 years), or when the renter makes certain modifications that the rental provider will have to reverse. Renters can challenge extra bond requests at VCAT, which considers whether paying would cause severe hardship.

heading: Reasons for claiming bond
text: The rental provider might claim the bond as compensation if the renter damaged the property, owes rent or charges, has not left the property reasonably clean, is missing items (for example, locks), or made certain changes to the property without asking. Rental providers cannot claim bond for fair wear and tear or for damage the rental provider was responsible for repairing.

heading: Final inspections
text: A rental provider, property manager or agent will do a final inspection at the end of the rental agreement. The condition report should be used to compare any changes to the property during the agreement. The renter must be present during the final inspection or have been given a reasonable opportunity to be there.

heading: Fair wear and tear
text: Fair wear and tear is deterioration because of reasonable use of the property or natural environmental forces. Faded curtains or worn kitchen bench tops are fair wear and tear, whereas ripped curtains or broken bench tops might be considered damage.

heading: Bond disputes
text: When renters and rental providers disagree about a bond claim, any party can apply to VCAT or Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV), who will hear the reasoning of each party and make the decision for them.

heading: How to claim a bond with the RTBA
text: Bonds are claimed using the RTBA website. Rental providers must start a claim within 14 days of the rental agreement ending, unless a renter starts a claim first. When a claim is submitted, every renter on the bond receives an email with a link to review and accept the claim. Renters must accept within 14 days or the claim expires.

heading: Claims with a VCAT or RDRV order
text: An order from VCAT or RDRV can be submitted to the RTBA, which will distribute the bond in accordance with the order within one business day after validating it.

heading: How the RTBA repays a bond
text: The RTBA repays bonds to nominated bank accounts, including international accounts. Account details must be accurate because the RTBA doesn't keep renters' banking details on record and can't double check them.

page_title: Leaving a rental property early (breaking the lease)
heading: What it means to break a rental agreement
text: Breaking a rental agreement means a renter leaves without giving notice, or leaves before the end of a fixed-term rental agreement.

page_title: Leaving a rental property early (breaking the lease)
heading: Reasons a renter can end early without paying costs
text: A renter can end the agreement early without paying costs, with the following minimum notice: the property did not meet the rental minimum standards when the renter moved in (immediate); a long-term agreement was verbal or not in the prescribed form (28 days); the rental provider refused disability-related modifications (14 days); the renter needs to move into special personal care (14 days); the renter is moving into social housing (14 days); the renter needs temporary crisis accommodation (14 days); the rental provider did not disclose before the agreement that the property was being sold (14 days). Documentary evidence is required for special circumstances. In other situations (for example, after the renter receives a notice to vacate for repairs, demolition, business use, owner or family occupation, sale or public purposes), the renter can leave with 14 days notice and VCAT may decide whether any costs apply.

page_title: Leaving a rental property early (breaking the lease)
heading: Costs for breaking an agreement
text: Renters must cover reasonable costs the rental provider incurs. Lost rent: VCAT decides the compensation; for fixed-term agreements of more than 5 years, compensation cannot be more than one month's rent for each 12 months remaining, up to a maximum of 6 months' rent. Renters don't owe rent once the property is re-let. Advertising costs: renters may have to pay reasonable re-advertising costs. Re-letting fees: renters usually pay a share based on how much of the agreement was left (for example, with 6 months of a 12-month agreement left, half the fee).

page_title: Leaving a rental property early (breaking the lease)
heading: Costs renters don't have to pay
text: Renters don't have to pay penalties for breaking the agreement, rent after the property is re-let, advertising fees if the property wasn't advertised, or re-letting fees if the owner let the property directly without an agent. Bond is repaid by agreement or VCAT order.

page_title: Leaving a rental property early (breaking the lease)
heading: Disputing costs and hardship
text: Renters should negotiate first; if they can't agree, either party can apply to VCAT. Renters facing severe hardship (such as job loss, a medical condition or a family tragedy) may apply to VCAT to end the agreement early, and VCAT must consider hardship when deciding compensation.

heading: When a notice to vacate can be challenged
text: A renter can challenge a notice to vacate if they believe it was not given to them properly or disagree with the reason given on the notice. Someone can also challenge a notice to vacate if they were experiencing family violence and the person using violence was the person whose behaviour resulted in the notice. If a renter does not leave after receiving a notice to vacate, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for a possession order, which can be enforced by police. A rental provider cannot personally evict a renter. Renters should ask for advice immediately, from Consumer Affairs Victoria or an advocacy service such as Tenants Victoria.

heading: How to challenge a notice to vacate
text: Renters who want to challenge a notice to vacate can apply to VCAT, which decides whether the notice was valid. If the challenge is not successful, the renter may have to pay the rental provider's VCAT application fee.

heading: Timeframes for challenging a notice to vacate
text: The renter must apply to VCAT within 30 days of getting a notice to vacate if the property is being repaired, being demolished, going to be used for business, going to be used by the rental provider or their family, going to be sold, or owned by a government authority that needs it for public use. If you have been given an immediate notice to vacate, there is no time limit to apply to VCAT, but you should apply as soon as possible; you can also challenge the notice at the VCAT hearing for the possession order.

heading: Challenging a notice to vacate because of family violence
text: If you are experiencing family violence and the person using violence caused the notice, you can apply to VCAT (within 30 days) if the notice was given for serious damage, danger, threats or intimidation, failing to comply with a VCAT order, a third breach of duty, illegal use, or drug-related activity in public housing.

heading: Contact
text: Consumer Affairs Victoria: 1300 55 81 81 (9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday), or the online enquiry form. Sections of the Act: 91ZZS – Renter may apply to Tribunal; 91ZZU – Renter may challenge notice to vacate on grounds of family violence or personal violence.

page_title: Challenging rent increases or high rent
heading: How to challenge a rent increase
text: Renters can ask Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate a rent increase they believe is above the market range, using the free rent assessment service. Renters can't be forced to leave a property because they ask for a rent assessment. Renters should first try to negotiate with their rental provider before asking for an investigation. All renters can request an assessment, including rooming house residents and caravan and residential park residents. Site tenants can only request a review if their site agreement allows non-fixed rent increases.

page_title: Challenging rent increases or high rent
heading: Timeline and process
text: A request must be made within 30 days of receiving the written notice of the rent increase, using the Request for Rental Assessment form. A case officer will contact the renter and an inspector may visit the property. After the investigation a report is given to both parties.

page_title: Challenging rent increases or high rent
heading: Challenging high rent without an increase
text: An assessment of rent that has not increased is only available in limited circumstances: when services or facilities previously provided have been removed without a matching reduction in rent, or when a rooming house resident's rent changes because room occupancy has increased.

page_title: Challenging rent increases or high rent
heading: What gets assessed
text: An assessment considers rent for comparable properties, the change in the consumer price index (CPI), the state of repair of the property, its location and facilities, when previous increases happened, and any relevant non-compliance with the law.

page_title: Challenging rent increases or high rent
heading: Next steps
text: If the assessment finds the rent is excessive and the rental provider will not negotiate, the renter can apply to Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria within 30 days, and the matter may go on to VCAT, which can make an order setting the rent.

heading: What is a condition report?
text: A condition report records the state of a rental property at the start of a rental agreement, including any issues with cleanliness, damage or things that don't work, covering fixtures, fittings and interior and exterior features. All rental properties, rooming houses, caravans, caravan sites and Part 4A park sites must have condition reports. The rental provider or their agent prepares and signs the report and gives the renter two paper copies (or one electronic copy) before the renter moves in. Condition reports are important evidence in disputes about bond claims, cleaning or who is responsible for damage.

heading: Condition reports at the start of the agreement
text: Rental providers must give the renter a signed condition report, using the official template, before the renter moves in. Renters should check it is accurate, add comments if needed, and return a signed copy within five business days. If no condition report is provided before the renter moves in, the renter may prepare their own and give it to the rental provider within the same timeframe. Taking dated, labelled photographs of the property at the start, especially of any existing damage, is recommended. Both parties should keep copies throughout the rental agreement.

heading: Disputes about the condition report
text: Either party may apply to VCAT within 30 days of the start of the rental agreement if they believe the condition report is inaccurate or incomplete.

heading: Condition reports at the end of the agreement
text: The rental provider or agent must complete the end-of-agreement section of the condition report within 10 days of the rental agreement ending, with the renter present or given a reasonable opportunity to attend. Rental providers may claim bond for new damage (beyond fair wear and tear), needed repairs, additional cleaning or missing items, supported by the condition report.

heading: Cleaning responsibilities
text: Renters must keep the property in a reasonably clean condition. When they leave, the property must be returned reasonably clean and in a similar condition to when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear. For agreements signed from 29 March 2021, rental providers cannot require professional cleaning at the end of the agreement unless professional cleaning is needed to return the property to the condition it was in at the start (allowing for fair wear and tear).

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Right of entry
text: Rental providers and their agents have the right to enter a property, but there are rules about the reasons they can enter and when. Renters must allow lawful entry when proper notice is given.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Reasons for entry and notice required
text: A rental provider may enter for: a general (routine) inspection – 7 days notice; repairs or to meet legal obligations – 24 hours notice; showing the property to prospective renters, buyers or lenders – 48 hours notice; a valuation – 7 days notice; taking photos or videos for advertising – 7 days notice; a suspected breach of the renter's obligations – 24 hours notice; family violence VCAT proceedings – 24 hours notice. The notice must be in writing and state the reason for entry.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Entry times
text: The rental provider or their agent can only enter the property between 8 am and 6 pm on any day except a public holiday.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: When renters can refuse entry
text: Renters may refuse entry if the visit is not between 8 am and 6 pm or is on a public holiday, no written notice was given, the notice was not properly delivered or did not give enough time, the rental provider wants to show the property to prospective renters outside the last 21 days of the agreement, or a general inspection has already been done in the past 6 months.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Conduct during entry
text: The rental provider must not enter in an unreasonable manner or stay longer than necessary for the purpose of the entry, unless the renter agrees. The renter does not need to be present if valid notice was given, and cannot be required to leave.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: General inspections
text: General inspections are only allowed after the first 3 months of the agreement and no more than once every 6 months.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Showing the property to prospective renters
text: The property can be shown to prospective renters when the renter has given a notice of intention to vacate or received a notice to vacate. Open inspections are limited to the last 21 days of the agreement, at most twice a week and one hour per visit unless the renter agrees otherwise.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Showing the property to prospective buyers or lenders
text: The rental provider must give at least 14 days notice using the Notice of intention to sell the property form before showing the property to buyers, and must make reasonable efforts to agree inspection times. Inspections are limited to twice a week, one hour per visit, unless the renter agrees. The renter must be compensated for each sales inspection: half a day's rent or $30, whichever is greater.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Photos and videos for advertising
text: Renters may object to photos or videos that could identify them or reveal sensitive information, show valuable items, or could identify people at risk of violence. If the renter objects, the rental provider cannot use that content. If the renter asks to review images before use, they cannot be published without the renter's written approval.

page_title: When a rental provider can enter a property
heading: Damage during entry
text: If something belonging to the renter is damaged or taken while the rental provider or agent is on the property, the renter may apply to VCAT for compensation.

page_title: Changing or ending the rental agreement because of family violence
heading: Changing or ending your rental agreement
text: If you are experiencing family violence and need to change your rental agreement to keep yourself or your children safe, you can apply to VCAT, whether or not your name is on the current agreement. Parents or guardians can also apply on behalf of children. You can ask VCAT to order the rental provider to create a new rental agreement in your name that excludes the person using violence, or to end the agreement early without penalty.

page_title: Changing or ending the rental agreement because of family violence
heading: Evidence VCAT considers
text: VCAT considers evidence such as family violence safety notices or intervention orders, personal safety intervention orders, financial records, photos, recordings or messages, and written statements from family, friends, support workers, health professionals, police, religious leaders, crisis accommodation providers, child protection staff, employers or lawyers. VCAT also weighs the risk to your or your children's safety and whether the person using violence has been arrested or has bail conditions. VCAT must hear these applications within three business days.

page_title: Changing or ending the rental agreement because of family violence
heading: After VCAT changes or ends the agreement
text: The rental provider may request a new condition report or inspection with proper notice. VCAT may decide how the bond is divided or remove the person using violence from the bond. An excluded person cannot enter the property but keeps some rights, such as being represented at inspections and applying to VCAT to end the agreement early.

page_title: Rental providers - gas and electrical safety
heading: Urgent gas and electrical repairs
text: Gas leaks, dangerous electrical faults, a failure of a supplied appliance for hot water, water, cooking, heating or laundry, and a failure of the gas, electricity or water supply are urgent repairs. If the rental provider cannot be reached or does not respond immediately, renters may arrange repairs up to $2,500 and be reimbursed within 7 days. Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include tiredness, shortness of breath, headaches, nausea, vomiting and dizziness.

page_title: Rental providers - gas and electrical safety
heading: Gas safety checks
text: For rental agreements entered into after 29 March 2021, rental providers must have a gas safety check done every 2 years by a licensed or registered gasfitter (endorsed for Type A Gas Appliances Servicing). If no check has been done in the past 2 years when a renter moves in, one must be done as soon as possible. Rental providers must tell renters the date of the last gas safety check and any outstanding recommendations before the agreement is entered into.

page_title: Rental providers - gas and electrical safety
heading: Electrical safety checks
text: For rental agreements entered into after 29 March 2021 (or fixed terms that become periodic after that date), all electrical installations and fittings must be checked by a licensed electrician at least once every 2 years, in accordance with AS/NZS 3019. From 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must connect to a switchboard-type circuit breaker and a switchboard-type residual current device. Rental providers must tell renters the date of the last electrical safety check before the agreement is entered into.

page_title: Rental providers - gas and electrical safety
heading: Records of safety checks
text: Rental providers must keep records of the most recent gas and electrical safety checks until the next check, and must give the renter a copy within 7 days of a written request.

heading: Informing a rental provider of late rent
text: If a renter is late paying their rent because they haven't paid by the due date, or has not paid at all, they are 'in arrears'. As a renter, you are responsible for paying your rent on time and as agreed in the rental agreement. If you know your rent is going to be late, try to speak to your rental provider as soon as possible and try to negotiate a new time to pay. Rental providers don't have to be flexible about payment amounts or dates and can take formal action against a renter who is late paying rent. However, it is illegal for a rental provider or agent to charge any sort of 'administration fee' or 'late fee' to process rent payments even if the rent is late.

heading: Rental provider can issue a notice to vacate for unpaid rent
text: If renters are more than 14 days late on rent (7 days for rooming house or caravan park residents), the rental provider can give them a notice to vacate. A notice to vacate must be given by hand, post or electronic communication (such as email); electronic communication can only be used if the renter has consented to receiving notices that way. A renter can challenge a notice to vacate by applying to VCAT. A rental provider, rooming house operator or park owner cannot personally evict a renter, physically or otherwise.

heading: Possession orders and payment plans
text: If a renter doesn't pay the late rent by the date in the notice to vacate, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for a possession order (an 'eviction notice'), which can be enforced by police. VCAT can issue the possession order or allow the renter (in special circumstances) to pay via a payment plan. If the parties agree on a payment plan and the renter pays as agreed, the possession order application will be dismissed and the rental agreement will continue. If the renter does not pay, the hearing can be fast-tracked and VCAT can issue the possession order.

heading: Limits on how often a renter can pay late
text: When a renter is given a notice to vacate because they have not paid rent, they can pay the rent owing by the vacate date stated on the notice to avoid eviction. Even if the matter goes to VCAT, if the amount is paid by the vacate date, the notice no longer applies. However, if more than four notices to vacate for unpaid rent are issued to a renter in a 12-month period, the renter has '4 strikes' against them; the strikes are cleared at the end of the 12 months if there are no more notices. If a fifth notice to vacate is given for unpaid rent, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for a possession order and VCAT can't dismiss the application solely because the renter could pay off the unpaid rent under a payment plan.

heading: Unpaid rent when the renter has died
text: When a sole renter dies, their next of kin or legal representative can deal with the rental provider to end the rental agreement. Rent doesn't need to be paid after the property has been vacated, even if it is before the end of the agreement. When a co-renter dies, the other renters are responsible for the rent.

heading: Sections of the Act
text: Section 91ZM – Non-payment of rent (residential rental agreement). Section 208 – Breach of duty notice.

heading: Rental properties must meet the minimum standards
text: There are 15 categories of minimum standards for rental properties, and all rental properties must meet the standards for each category. Rental providers and agents must make sure a property meets minimum standards at the time they advertise or offer to let the property, and before the renter moves in. There are special rules for minimum standards in rooming houses.

heading: When minimum standards apply
text: Rental properties must meet the minimum standards before they are advertised. For existing rental agreements, the minimum standards in Schedule 4 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 apply if the agreement started on or after 29 March 2021, or started before 29 March 2021 and became a periodic (month to month) agreement on or after 29 March 2021. They don't apply if the agreement became periodic before 29 March 2021. New minimum rental standards for energy efficiency come into effect from 1 March 2027.

heading: Bathrooms
text: A bathroom must have a washbasin and a shower or bath, connected to a reasonable supply of hot and cold water. Showers must have a shower head with a 3-star water efficiency rating; if one cannot be installed, a 1- or 2-star shower head is acceptable.

heading: Electrical safety
text: The electrical safety standard commenced on 29 March 2023. Rental properties must have modern switchboards, with circuit breakers and electrical safety switches (residual current devices: RCD, RCCB or RCBO) installed. Rental providers are responsible for engaging an electrician to make the property comply. Older properties with fuse boards may need the entire switchboard replaced.

heading: Heating
text: All rental properties must have a fixed heater (not portable) in good working order in the main living area. For rental agreements entered into from 29 March 2023, this must be an energy efficient fixed heater: a non-ducted air conditioner or heat pump with a 2 star or above energy rating, a gas space heater with a 2 star or above energy rating, a ducted or hydronic heating system with an outlet in the main living area, or a solid fuel appliance such as a fireplace or wood burning stove. In some apartments it may be unreasonable to install an energy efficient heater (for example because of cost or owners corporation rules); a fixed heater must still be installed and the renter told before signing.

heading: Kitchen
text: The property must have a kitchen with a dedicated cooking and food preparation area, a sink in good working order connected to a reasonable supply of hot and cold water, and a stovetop in good working order with two or more burners. If there is an oven, it must be in good working order.

heading: Laundry and lighting
text: If there is a laundry, it must be connected to a reasonable supply of hot and cold water. Inside rooms, corridors and hallways must have access to light: natural light during the day (which can be borrowed from an adjoining room) and artificial light at night.

heading: Locks
text: External entry doors must have functioning deadlocks (a deadlatch with at least one cylinder), or locks that can be unlocked with a key from the outside but without a key from the inside. Exceptions include doors that cannot be secured with a deadlock, screen doors in the same frame as an external door, and doors behind another security barrier.

heading: Mould and damp, structural soundness
text: All rooms must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. The property must be structurally sound and weatherproof.

heading: Toilets and ventilation
text: The toilet must be in good working order, connected to a sewerage system, approved wastewater system or council-approved system, and be in a separate room (by itself or in a bathroom or combined bathroom-laundry). All habitable rooms, including bathroom, shower, toilet and laundry, must have adequate ventilation meeting the Building Code of Australia.

heading: Vermin proof bins
text: Rental providers must supply a rubbish bin and a recycling bin that are vermin proof and meet council collection standards.

heading: Windows, window coverings and anchors
text: All external windows that can open must have a functioning latch to secure them against external entry and must be able to be left open or closed. Windows in rooms likely to be used as bedrooms or living areas must have curtains or blinds that can be closed, block light and provide privacy. From 1 December 2025, all corded internal window coverings, such as blinds and curtains, must have an anchor installed to secure the cords and prevent them forming loops.

page_title: New changes to the rental laws
heading: Overview
text: New rules are making renting fairer and more secure for Victorians. If you're renting, you'll have stronger rights and protections, greater security over your lease and finances and improved safety in your home. If you're a rental provider, you'll have clearer obligations and better processes for managing your property.

page_title: New changes to the rental laws
heading: Upcoming changes from 13 October 2026
text: Strengthened bond claims: rental providers must notify the renter in advance if they will be making a claim on the bond at the end of the rental agreement and must provide evidence to support the claim. Records showing compliance with rental minimum standards: documentation demonstrating property compliance must be retained and provided to Consumer Affairs Victoria upon request. Mandatory gas and electrical safety checks every 2 years: rental providers and their agents must arrange gas and electrical safety checks by a qualified tradesperson every two years for all rental agreements. Gas check before draughtproofing: a licensed gasfitter inspection is required within 6 months prior to draughtproofing work. Ban on rental provider and agent application fees: it will be an offence for the rental provider or agent to charge a renter fees to make a rental application.

page_title: New changes to the rental laws
heading: Upcoming changes phased from 1 March 2027
text: New minimum energy efficiency standards: properties must meet standards covering heating, cooling, hot water systems, showerheads, ceiling insulation and draughtproofing, with phased implementation.

page_title: New changes to the rental laws
heading: Changes in effect from 25 November 2025
text: Ban on no fault evictions: rental providers cannot issue a renter with a notice to vacate without a valid reason, even at the end of a fixed-term agreement. Fixed-term agreements automatically convert to periodic agreements when they expire unless a new agreement is made. Extended notice periods: rental providers must give a renter 90 days' notice of a rent increase and certain notices to vacate. Ban on all types of rental bidding: agents and rental providers are banned from accepting offers made by a renter to pay rent higher than the advertised amount or to pay more than one month's rent in advance. Minimum standards at advertising: it is an offence for a rental provider or their agent to advertise a property that does not meet the minimum standards. Mandatory annual smoke alarm checks: rental providers and their agents must arrange annual smoke alarm safety checks for all rental agreements. Protection of renters' personal information: it is an offence to disclose information without consent.

page_title: New changes to the rental laws
heading: Changes in effect from 1 December 2025
text: Blind cord safety anchors: all rental properties must have secured cords on internal window coverings to prevent them forming loops. Rooming house heating standard: fixed heaters must be installed in each resident's room.

page_title: New changes to the rental laws
heading: Changes in effect from 31 March 2026
text: New standard rental application form: prescribed forms must be used for rental applications. Information collection rules: rental providers are limited to requesting information necessary to assess suitability and verify identity and capacity to pay rent. Ban on third party application and payment fees: rental providers and agents may still use third party platforms, but it is an offence for the businesses that run these to charge a renter fees. Rent increase investigation factors: the matters the Director and the Tribunal consider when deciding whether a rent increase is excessive have been expanded.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: What is a notice to vacate?
text: When a rental provider (landlord) wants a renter to move out, they can talk to the renter to reach an agreement or give the renter a notice to vacate. A notice to vacate is a formal statement that the rental provider wants to end the rental agreement, and can only be given for certain reasons. If a renter does not leave by the termination date in the notice, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for a possession order.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Reasons rental providers can and cannot give notice
text: Rental providers can only give notice for the reasons listed below; other reasons are not valid. A rental provider must give a reason and cannot give notice without a valid reason. A rental provider cannot give someone notice for doing something, or saying they will do something, they are legally allowed to do: for example, a rental provider cannot give a renter a notice to vacate for requesting repairs, asking to have a pet, or challenging a rent increase. A notice to vacate is not valid if it is unlawful discrimination. A rental provider may ask a renter to leave without giving a notice to vacate; the renter does not have to agree.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Immediate notice
text: A rental provider can give a notice to vacate immediately if the renter or their visitor intentionally or recklessly causes serious damage to the property, including safety equipment and common areas, or puts neighbours, the rental provider, the agent, or their contractors or employees in danger.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: How to give a notice to vacate
text: Rental providers should use the Notice to vacate to renter/s of rented premises form. The notice must be addressed to the renter, give the reason for ending the agreement, be signed by the rental provider or agent, be sent with enough time to reach the renter, and state the termination date. It must be delivered by registered post, by hand, or by electronic communication (such as email) if the renter has consented to receive notices that way.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Challenging a notice to vacate
text: A renter can challenge a notice to vacate if they believe it was not given properly, disagree with the reason given, or were given the notice as a result of family violence. If a renter does not leave after being given notice, the rental provider can apply for a possession order.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Ending an agreement early: reasons and notice periods
text: A rental provider can only end a rental agreement before its end date for these reasons (minimum notice in brackets): the renter or visitor intentionally or recklessly causes serious damage (immediate); the renter or visitor puts others in danger (immediate); the premises are unfit for human habitation or destroyed (immediate); the renter or anyone living there seriously threatens or intimidates the rental provider, agent, contractors or employees (14 days); the renter owes at least 14 days rent (14 days); the renter has failed to comply with a VCAT compliance order (14 days); the renter has already been given 2 breach of duty notices and the same breach occurs again (14 days); the property is used for illegal purposes (14 days); the renter has brought in other renters or sub-letters without consent (14 days); the renter has not paid the bond as agreed (14 days); a child under 16 lives there when the agreement says this is not allowed (14 days); the renter misled a government housing authority to get social housing (14 days); drug-related activity in public housing (14 days); the renter is keeping a pet without consent and VCAT has made an order excluding the pet (28 days).

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Notice to vacate at the end of a fixed term or during a periodic agreement
text: Rental providers cannot issue a notice to vacate at the end of a fixed term agreement without a valid reason. Generally, the standard notice for a valid reason is 90 days, but in some situations it can be less. For a fixed-term agreement, the termination date must be on or after the end date of the agreement. For a periodic (month-by-month) agreement, a notice to vacate can be issued at any time, provided it is for a valid reason. Some reasons require evidence to be supplied with the notice; if required evidence is not supplied, the notice is invalid.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Valid reasons, evidence and notice periods
text: The rental provider plans to move in at the end of the fixed term, where this was listed in the additional terms of the agreement (section 91ZW): evidence is the rental agreement and a witnessed statutory declaration by each rental provider; 14 days notice. Reconstruction, repairs or renovations that cannot go ahead unless the renter leaves: evidence is photos and a tradesperson's contract or quote, or a building permit (only a building permit is sufficient for renovations); 90 days notice (previously 60 days). Demolition: building permit and contract with a builder-demolisher; 90 days notice; the premises must not be re-let as a residence for 6 months unless VCAT approves. Use for another purpose such as a business: statutory declaration plus ABN, business registration or planning permit; 90 days notice. The rental provider, their immediate family (including parents and parents-in-law) or a dependant will move in: witnessed statutory declaration naming the person; 90 days notice; the premises must not be re-let to anyone else for 6 months unless VCAT approves. The property is to be sold or put up for sale and vacated at the end of the agreement: contract of sale, agent's authority to sell, or a contract prepared by a conveyancer or lawyer; 90 days notice; the rental provider cannot shorten the agreement for this reason and must not re-let the premises as a residence for 6 months unless VCAT approves. A government authority needs the property for public purposes: acquisition details or letter; 90 days notice. The renter no longer meets social housing eligibility criteria: 90 days notice.

page_title: Notice to vacate in rental properties
heading: Mortgagee and deceased renter
text: A mortgagee (lender) repossessing the property can give a renter a notice to vacate under specific provisions. If a sole renter dies, the rental provider can end the agreement by giving a notice to vacate to the renter's legal personal representative or next of kin.

heading: Overview
text: Pests, infestations, mould and damp can harm people's health and damage property if not dealt with quickly. In extreme cases they are an urgent repair. Pests and infestations might include mice, rats, possums, fleas, ants or termites. Renters who see signs of pests, infestations, mould or rising damp should tell the rental provider immediately.

heading: Who is responsible
text: The law doesn't always say who is responsible; it can depend on who contributed to the problem. If the issue comes from the building structure, the renter can request an urgent repair. The renter may be responsible if their actions contributed, for example not using the bathroom ventilation fan leading to mould, not removing rubbish that attracted ants, mice or cockroaches, or not treating their pet for fleas. The rental provider may be responsible if a problem with the property caused mould or damp or let pests in, for example broken window frames letting rain in, pests present when the renter moved in, or holes in the roof. If there is disagreement about who pays, either party can apply to VCAT.

heading: When pests or mould are an urgent repair
text: If pests or mould caused by or related to the building structure make the property unsafe or unsecure to live in, they are an urgent repair. Renters may need to provide proof the mould is dangerous, such as an assessment report by an occupational hygienist, environmental health professional or council, or a doctor's report for people with existing health conditions such as asthma. Renters may apply to VCAT to recover the cost of health assessments or medical reports.

heading: Overview
text: Renters who want to have a pet in the property must ask their rental provider (landlord) for permission. Rental providers must have a good reason to refuse the renter's request, and can apply to VCAT for an order to refuse permission. All renters, including those with pets, must keep the property clean, avoid damage and not be a nuisance to others. A pet means any animal except an assistance dog, which is a dog trained to help a person with a disability. Assistance dogs do not count as pets, and people with assistance dogs cannot be discriminated against.

heading: Pet requests
text: Renters who want to keep a pet should complete a Pet request form (a separate form for each pet), give it to the rental provider and keep a copy. The rental provider has 14 days (starting the day after they receive the form) to make a decision. If they agree, they should give consent in writing. If they don't agree, they must apply to VCAT and tell the renter they have done so within the 14 days; the renter can't keep the pet while VCAT is making a decision. If the rental provider does not respond at all within the 14 days, the renter can keep the pet. Renters should also check that the pet complies with local council laws, which apply whether or not the rental provider has given consent.

heading: Negotiating conditions for keeping a pet
text: The rental provider can try to negotiate conditions for keeping a pet, for example that the pet is not allowed inside. If the renter does not agree to the conditions and the rental provider wants to exclude the pet, they must apply to VCAT. Any agreed conditions should be put in writing.

heading: VCAT's role
text: If the rental provider applies to VCAT, VCAT can order that the refusal is reasonable and/or the pet is excluded, or that the renter can keep the pet. VCAT may consider the type of pet, the type of property, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, other relevant laws such as council laws, and anything else it considers relevant. If VCAT makes an order excluding the pet, the renter has 14 days to comply. If the renter has not complied after that, the rental provider can give them a notice to vacate with a minimum of 28 days' notice.

heading: Pets causing damage
text: If a renter does not meet their duties (for example a pet causes damage), the rental provider can give them a Notice of breach of duty. If the renter does not comply, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for a compensation or compliance order. VCAT will consider fair wear and tear and the age and condition of the damaged items. If a rental provider reasonably believes a renter is keeping a pet without consent, they can apply to VCAT for an order to exclude the pet.

heading: Pet bonds
text: Rental providers and owners cannot ask for an additional bond as a 'pet bond'.

heading: Pets in apartments and units
text: If the property is an apartment or unit, the owners corporation may have its own rules about pets in common areas, which the renter must follow. If the owners corporation decides the pet is dangerous or is causing a nuisance, the renter may have to remove the pet.

heading: Rules for increasing rent
text: A rental provider (landlord) can increase the rent for their property, but there are rules about what they can do. The rental provider is not allowed to increase the rent during a fixed term agreement unless the rental agreement (lease) has an additional clause (term) allowing for an increase. If this is the case, the agreement must also state how the increase will be calculated. To put the rent up, the rental provider must give the renter (tenant) a Notice of proposed rent increase via the method agreed to in the rental agreement at least 90 days in advance. If you are serving a notice by post, read Australia Post's delivery time estimates information. These rules apply to people living in rented residential premises, rooming houses and caravan parks. However, if you rent in a residential park, there are different rules for rent increases under a site agreement. Important: If the rent increase rules are not followed the increase may be invalid. Renters can challenge a rent increase if they think it is higher than the market range. There are also limits on how often the rent can be increased.

heading: How much rent can increase
text: The law doesn't say exactly how much a rental provider can put the rent up by. However, the law does require a rental provider to give their renter information about how they have calculated the rent increase. A rental provider can't increase the rent during a fixed term agreement unless the rental agreement (lease) says this is okay. If the rental agreement allows for an increase during the fixed term, the agreement must state how the increase will be calculated. In other cases, the rental provider still must give the renter information about how the increase is calculated. The rental provider must inform the renter using a Notice of rent increase form. This form must be given to the renter at least 90 days before the increase is due to start. The 4 most common methods for calculating a rent increase are: according to how much prices are generally changing in the economy, known as the consumer price index (CPI); according to average rent prices in Victoria, known as the metropolitan rent index or the regional rent index; by a fixed percentage increase (e.g. 3%); by a fixed dollar amount (e.g. $10). Rental providers can use other approaches if they prefer. Simply referring to a method in the rental agreement is not enough. The rent increase information in the rental agreement and in the Notice of rent increase must be sufficiently clear so the renter can work out how rent increases will be calculated and if the increase matches what is specified in the agreement.

heading: Examples of invalid and valid wording
text: Invalid wording (invalid increase): "Rent increased by dollar amount"; "Based on the rental market valuation"; "As per rental provider's instructions"; "All properties in the same building are leased between (price range)"; "CPI". Valid wording (examples only): "The next rent increase will be by 1.8% in line with the Consumer Price Index increase as reported by the Australian Bureau of Statistics for the September 2025 quarter." "The next rent increase will be by $20 in line with the statewide rent increase for the June 2025 quarter." If a rental provider relies on an estate agent to manage their rental property, the agent will also need to prepare the Notice of rent increase form correctly. If you are a renter and you think the rent increase is invalid you can request a review.

heading: How often rent can increase
text: A rental provider can only increase the rent at certain times. In most cases, rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months, even if the rental agreement specifies a rent increase before that time. Agreements shorter than 5 years: rental providers must wait until the end of the rental agreement to increase the rent, unless the agreement says otherwise. If the agreement does say rent can be increased during the fixed term: for agreements that started before 19 June 2019, the rent can't be increased more than once every 6 months; for rental agreements that started on or after 19 June 2019, the rent can't be increased more than once every 12 months. Agreements longer than 5 years (long-term rental agreements): rent must not be increased more than once every 12 months, and only if the agreement says that the rent can be increased. Periodic (month by month) agreements: for periodic rental agreements that started before 19 June 2019, the rent can't be increased more than once every 6 months; for rental agreements that became periodic on or after 19 June 2019, the rent can't be increased more than once every 12 months. This is true even if it has been month by month for several years. If the rental provider increases the rent, the renter can accept the increase, ask for a rent assessment or tell the rental provider they want to end the agreement and leave (a notice of intention to vacate).

heading: Telling renters about rent increases
text: Rental providers must tell renters about rent increases at least 90 days before they are going to put the rent up, and they must use the Notice of rent increase form. The rental provider must tell the renter how much the rent will increase, how the rental provider calculated the rent increase, and what the renter can do if they think the increase is too high. Rent can't be increased unless the rental provider has used the right form. If the rental provider doesn't use the right form, the notice isn't valid. The renter only has to pay the increase if they are given proper notice.

heading: Rent can't be increased to penalise a renter
text: A rental provider can't ask a renter to pay more rent because they have broken any part of the rental agreement. Rental agreements can't include anything that says a renter has to pay more rent if they break any of the terms of the rental agreement. There are financial penalties if the rental provider includes a prohibited term like this in the agreement, and such a term can't be enforced.

heading: Changes to the bond when rent increases
text: Additional bond amounts can only be required for rent increases when there is a long-term agreement which is being renewed for another fixed term of more than 5 years. The rental provider must give the renter 120 days written notice using the Notice requesting additional bond, and the renter must pay the additional bond amount within these 120 days. The rental provider can't do this more than once every 5 years. Additional bond amounts cannot be required for a periodic or fixed short-term agreement. The rental provider must lodge the additional bond with the RTBA within 10 business days after receiving it. The renter can apply to VCAT to change the rental agreement so that extra bond can't be required, or to change the amount of extra bond.

page_title: Rent payments and rent in advance
heading: Methods of payment
text: A rental agreement must specify the rent amount and payment frequency. Rent must be paid to the rental provider according to the terms of the agreement. The renter and rental provider should agree on payment methods before the agreement starts. The rental provider must provide at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees), must allow payment by Commonwealth Centrepay and by electronic funds transfer, must disclose any fees associated with the chosen payment method, and cannot require post-dated cheques. Neither party can require reimbursement for account set-up or payment processing costs.

page_title: Rent payments and rent in advance
heading: Illegal fees and charges
text: Rental providers cannot charge fees for issuing payment cards, setting up or using direct debit, processing payments, or late payment of rent. Third-party platforms used to manage rental agreements cannot charge renters fees (standard bank fees excluded).

page_title: Rent payments and rent in advance
heading: Payment frequency and timing
text: Rental agreements specify the payment schedule: weekly, fortnightly, calendar monthly, or another agreed time. Renters paying by electronic transfer should allow 24 hours so the payment is not treated as late.

page_title: Rent payments and rent in advance
heading: Charging rent in advance
text: Rental providers cannot ask for more than one month's rent in advance. Exceptions: if rent is paid weekly, the maximum rent in advance is 14 days; if the rent is more than $900 a week, there is no limit. Rooming houses, caravan parks and Part 4A sites have additional restrictions capping rent in advance at between 14 and 28 days depending on the type of property.

page_title: Rent payments and rent in advance
heading: Stopping rent payments
text: Renters must not stop paying rent until they agree with their rental provider on the date payments stop. The obligation to pay rent continues even if there are problems with repairs, the lease is ending, or a notice to vacate has been given.

page_title: Rent payments and rent in advance
heading: Providing rent receipts
text: A receipt must be provided immediately if rent is paid in person, or within five business days if the renter asks for one. A receipt must include the rental provider's name and signature, the property address, the date of payment and the period the payment covers, the amount paid, and clearly state that it is a receipt. Records of rent payments must be kept for at least 12 months.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Overview
text: There are rules about the changes renters can make to a property, and they will often need permission from the rental provider. The rules depend on the type of change, the type of rental property and the length of the rental agreement. A rental provider may require that changes are done by a suitably qualified person.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Changes that can be made without permission
text: A renter can install the following without permission: non-permanent window film for insulation, reduced heat transfer or privacy; a wireless doorbell; curtains (without throwing out the original curtains); adhesive child safety locks on drawers and doors; pressure mounted child safety gates; a lock on a letterbox. If the property is not on the Victorian Heritage Register, a renter can also install without permission: picture hooks or screws for wall mounts, shelves or brackets on any surface except exposed brick or concrete walls; wall anchors to secure furniture (except on exposed brick or concrete); LED light bulbs that don't need new fittings; low flow shower heads (keeping the original); blind or cord anchors; removable safety devices such as alarm systems or security cameras that don't affect neighbours' privacy, can be easily removed and are not hardwired; hardware mounted child safety gates (except on exposed brick or concrete).

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Reasonable changes the rental provider cannot unreasonably refuse
text: For any other change the renter must ask permission, but the rental provider cannot refuse the following without a good reason: picture hooks, wall anchors or hardware mounted child safety gates on exposed brick or concrete walls; draughtproofing in a property without open flued gas heating; a security system installed by a suitably qualified person (with an invoice naming the installer); flyscreens on doors and windows; a vegetable or herb garden; a secure letterbox; painting the premises; modifications to secure external gates; conservation work on a registered heritage place. Nor can they unreasonably refuse changes that don't penetrate or permanently change surfaces or structure, are needed for health and safety, are disability-related modifications recommended by an occupational therapist, give access to phone, internet or TV, are reasonable security measures, are needed for the safety of a renter experiencing family violence or protected by a personal safety intervention order, keep the renter from being too hot or cold, or reduce energy and water bills.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Reasons a rental provider can refuse changes
text: It might be reasonable to refuse if heritage protections would be affected, the change would breach other legal requirements, it would significantly change the property, it would require changes to other premises or common areas, it would add maintenance costs if not reversed, reversing it is not reasonably practicable, or the property is about to be sold or vacated and a valid notice to vacate has been given.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Modification bond
text: The rental provider may require an extra bond (a modification bond) to cover the cost of undoing changes at the end of the agreement. They cannot ask for it if the extra bond would be less than $500, if it is unreasonable compared with the cost of reversing the changes, if the rental provider does not want the changes reversed, or if the changes are funded by a scheme such as the NDIS where restoration is not required.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: If the rental provider does not agree
text: The renter should first ask why the request was refused. If the renter thinks the rental provider is refusing reasonable changes, they can apply to VCAT for a ruling.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Short-term and long-term agreements
text: In a short-term agreement (5 years or less), apart from the allowed list a renter must not make changes without permission; if they do, the rental provider can give a Notice of breach of duty requiring the renter to restore the property or pay the reasonable cost of restoring it. Even if a rental provider gives permission for changes, they do not have to pay for them. In a long-term agreement, changes can be agreed and written into the agreement before signing. Before the end of the agreement, a renter who has made changes must restore the property (allowing for fair wear and tear) or pay the reasonable cost of restoring it, unless the rental provider agrees otherwise, the agreement says so, or the renter paid a modification bond.

page_title: Renters making changes to the property
heading: Safety devices
text: Renters must not remove, deactivate or interfere with safety devices such as smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms, electrical safety switches or pool barriers, except where reasonable (for example dusting a smoke alarm or silencing it after an accidental activation). Renters must not take the batteries out of a smoke alarm.

heading: The difference between urgent and non-urgent repairs
text: A repair is non-urgent if the renter can continue to safely live in the property. Examples of non-urgent repairs include a broken dishwasher or loose bathroom tiles. Anything not on the urgent repairs list is a non-urgent repair.

heading: List of urgent repairs
text: Urgent repairs must be done immediately. The legally defined urgent repairs are: a burst water service; a blocked or broken toilet system; a serious roof leak; a gas leak; a dangerous electrical fault; flooding or serious flood damage; serious storm or fire damage; a failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, water, cooking, heating or laundering; a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply; a failure or breakdown of a cooling appliance or service provided by the rental provider; the property not meeting the rental minimum standards; a safety-related device (such as a smoke alarm or pool fence) not working; an appliance, fitting or fixture that is broken and causing a lot of water to be wasted; a building fault that causes pests, mould or damp; and a serious problem with a lift or staircase.

heading: Organising and paying for repairs
text: Rental providers must organise and pay for all repairs if the damage is not the renter's fault. Renters should tell the rental provider about repairs in writing as soon as possible. For urgent repairs, renters must contact the rental provider immediately, using the emergency phone number provided at the start of the agreement, and confirm the request in writing.

heading: Renter options for urgent repairs
text: If the rental provider doesn't respond to an urgent repair request, the renter can organise and pay for the repair themselves if it costs no more than $2,500. The rental provider must pay the renter back within 7 days. For urgent repairs costing more than $2,500, renters should apply to Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV).

heading: Non-urgent repairs
text: Written repair requests should include the date. Rental providers must complete non-urgent repairs within 14 days of the date of the written request.

heading: Who can make a repair
text: Work that requires a licence must be done by a qualified professional. All repairs must be made to the standard a tradesperson would make them, whether they are done by the renter or the rental provider.

heading: Paying rent during repairs
text: Renters must continue paying rent while waiting for repairs. However, they can apply to RDRV to have their rent paid into a special account held by Consumer Affairs Victoria (the Rent Special Account) until the matter is resolved.

heading: When the rental provider does not respond
text: Renters should keep records of their attempts to contact the rental provider. If a non-urgent repair has not been done within 14 days, renters can request a free repairs inspection from Consumer Affairs Victoria, which can direct the rental provider to complete the work.

heading: Rules when the renter is at fault
text: If the renter caused the damage, the rental provider must give a written repair notice specifying the damage and whether the renter should repair it or the rental provider will repair it at the renter's expense. If the renter organises the repair, the work must be completed within 14 days to a tradesperson's standard.

heading: Efficient replacements
text: When replacing water, gas or electrical appliances, rental providers must choose items that meet minimum efficiency standards.

heading: Resolving repair disputes
text: Renters can request a free repairs inspection when there is a dispute about who caused the damage for a non-urgent repair, or when the rental provider ignores repair requests. RDRV is a free alternative dispute resolution service that handles repair disputes, by phone, online or in person at VCAT offices. If RDRV doesn't resolve the dispute, renters can apply to VCAT for a compensation order or repair order.

heading: Entry for repairs
text: Rental providers must give at least 24 hours notice to enter the property for repairs, and can only enter between 8am and 6pm on a day that is not a public holiday. Urgent repairs may be an exception if the renter agrees.

heading: Rental agreements
text: A rental agreement used to be called a lease or residential tenancy agreement. It is a contract between the renter and rental provider. A rental agreement should include the amount of rent and how it is paid, how rent increases will be calculated, the length and type of agreement, the bond amount, other conditions and rules, and any special terms. The prescribed form must be used for a written rental agreement. Extra terms can be added if they are not prohibited, but terms cannot take away rights and responsibilities provided by the law. There is no cooling-off period for a rental agreement.

heading: Types of residential rental agreements
text: There are 3 types: short fixed-term agreements, long fixed-term agreements, and periodic (month to month) agreements. Short fixed-term agreements are usually 6 or 12 months but can be up to 5 years; they can be written or verbal, but written agreements are recommended (Form 1). If a fixed-term agreement ends and the renter stays without signing a further agreement, it automatically turns into a periodic (month to month) agreement, and for agreements of 5 years or less the terms of the original agreement continue to apply.

heading: Long fixed-term agreements
text: Long fixed-term agreements are for more than 5 years (Form 2). Different rules include bond top-ups after 5 years when renewed for another 5 or more years, agreeing modifications before signing, and a cap on costs for leaving early of one month's rent for every full year remaining, up to a maximum of 6 months. Long-term agreements must be in writing; if not, the renter can end the agreement at any time by giving the rental provider 28 days' notice.

heading: Before moving in
text: Before a renter moves in, the rental provider or agent must give them a copy of the written rental agreement, a copy of the Renters guide, an emergency phone number for urgent repairs, the rental provider or agent's full name, postal address and (if agreed) email address, a set of keys for each renter who signed the agreement, and a condition report (2 copies or 1 electronic).

heading: Conditions that cannot be in an agreement
text: Renters cannot be required to take out any form of insurance; pay additional rent or penalties if they break the rules; pay for preparing the agreement; pay rent in advance in a way that costs extra (other than bank fees); use a third-party service provider nominated by the rental provider (other than an embedded network); pay for or organise maintenance of the rental provider's safety equipment; or indemnify the rental provider. The agreement cannot say that rent will be reduced or rebates paid if the renter does not break the rules; that the renter is bound by a contract they did not agree to in writing; that the renter cannot claim compensation if the premises are not available on the start date; that the renter must pay the rental provider's VCAT filing costs or insurance excess; or that the renter must pay a fixed break fee unless the basis for calculating it is set out in the agreement. A prohibited term is not valid and the rental provider may face penalties.

heading: Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria
text: Renters, rental providers and estate agents can use Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV), a free alternative dispute resolution service offered by VCAT. RDRV can help resolve disputes about many renting issues, including rent increases, repairs and bonds. If RDRV can't resolve the issue, it will help you apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). RDRV can be contacted by phone, online or in person at any VCAT office. Each application is case managed by a resolution coordinator, and methods include facilitated discussions and mediation.

heading: Steps to resolving a renting dispute
text: 1. Know your rights and responsibilities. 2. Talk to your agent or rental provider. 3. Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria. If still unresolved, apply to RDRV. Common dispute topics are bond claims, rental agreements, repairs and maintenance, rent increases, notices to vacate and goods left behind. Urgent issues needing immediate contact include illegal evictions and urgent repairs not addressed by the rental provider.

heading: Talking about and documenting disputes
text: Explain the problem and the outcome you want, and which obligations you believe are not being met. Record any agreement in writing. If you can't agree, put complaints in writing or, if applicable, issue a breach of duty notice. When someone breaks the rental agreement in a way that is a breach of duty, a formal breach of duty notice can be the first step.

heading: Going to VCAT
text: If RDRV cannot resolve the case, it can help you apply to VCAT, which resolves disputes when other steps have not worked. You will need evidence such as letters, emails, phone records, photos, videos or receipts.

heading: Further help
text: Financially disadvantaged renters or those experiencing family violence can contact the Tenancy Assistance and Advocacy Program. Renters facing eviction for rent arrears can use Dear Landlord, a free Justice Connect self-help tool. Consumer Affairs Victoria cannot help with disputes between renters; contact the Dispute Settlement Centre of Victoria. Renters aged 55 and over can contact Housing for the Aged Action Group (HAAG).

heading: Rental providers must fit smoke alarms
text: Smoke alarms are compulsory in all Victorian residential properties, and rental providers must ensure their property is fitted with them. Buildings constructed after 1 August 1997 must have hard-wired smoke alarms with battery back-up; older buildings can have battery-powered smoke alarms. Smoke alarms must meet Australian Standard AS 3786. Rooming houses must have hard-wired smoke alarms.

heading: Rental providers must make sure smoke alarms are working
text: Rental providers must ensure all smoke alarms are correctly installed and working, are fitted with batteries or replacement batteries, and are tested at least once every 12 months according to the manufacturer's instructions. On or before the start of a rental agreement, the rental provider must give the renter written information about how each smoke alarm operates, how to test it, and the renter's obligation not to tamper with smoke alarms and to report any that are not working.

heading: Renters and smoke alarms
text: Renters must tell the rental provider if a smoke alarm is faulty or not working. Renters must not deactivate, remove or interfere with a smoke alarm; doing so is a breach of duty and the rental provider may give a Notice of breach of duty. When renters move out, they should leave the batteries in the smoke alarm.

heading: Broken smoke alarms are urgent repairs
text: If told that a smoke alarm is not working, rental providers must immediately arrange for it to be repaired or replaced as an urgent repair. If the rental provider cannot be contacted or does not fix it immediately, the renter can authorise and pay for an urgent repair of up to $2,500, and the rental provider must pay them back within 7 days. A hard-wired smoke alarm must be installed by a qualified electrician, but anyone can change a smoke alarm battery.

heading: Water tanks in bushfire prone areas
text: For agreements entered into after 29 March 2021, if a property is in a bushfire prone area and a water tank is required for firefighting, the rental provider must ensure the tank is maintained in good repair and is clean and full at the start of the agreement.

heading: Protected characteristics
text: In Victoria it is against the law to stop somebody renting a property because of certain personal characteristics, including age; carer status, family responsibilities or parental status; disability; employment; gender identity, lawful sexual activity or sexual orientation; marital status; physical features; pregnancy or breastfeeding; profession, trade or occupation (including being a sex worker); race (including colour, nationality, ethnicity and ethnic origin); religious belief or activity; and sex. Sexual harassment is also against the law. A person who believes they have been discriminated against can contact the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission (VEOHRC) or apply to VCAT for compensation. Rental providers must give applicants a prescribed statement of information on discrimination.

heading: Children and renting
text: A rental provider or agent cannot refuse to rent to someone because a child (under 16) will live with them. The only exceptions are if the property is the rental provider's main residence or is unsuitable for children. A person who disagrees that a property is unsuitable can apply to VCAT.

heading: Renters with disability and assistance dogs
text: Rental providers must not discriminate against renters who have or acquire a disability, and should not refuse reasonable changes to the property. People with assistance dogs cannot be discriminated against, asked to remove the dog, asked to leave, or charged extra because of the dog.

heading: Pets and first-time renters
text: It is not unlawful discrimination to refuse to rent to someone with a pet, although rental providers can't unreasonably refuse a renter's request to keep a pet. Having never rented before is also not a protected characteristic.

heading: Water and sewerage
text: Renters in properties with individual water meters must pay for water usage and sewage disposal, unless the rental provider agrees otherwise in the rental agreement. Rental providers remain responsible for infrastructure (supply) charges and for maintaining water tanks, unless the renter caused the damage.

heading: Electricity, gas and oil
text: Rental providers must pay for installing and connecting electricity, gas or oil supply. Where the supply is metered, renters pay for usage unless the rental agreement says otherwise. Renters pay for bottled gas.

heading: Phone and internet
text: Renters must pay for the ongoing usage costs for phone and internet, unless the rental provider agrees otherwise. Rental providers pay for the initial installation of a connection, but renters may be charged reconnection fees for an existing line.

heading: Television
text: Television is not an essential service. Renters may ask for an antenna to be installed but rental providers don't have to do it.

heading: Excessive usage charges
text: Rental providers pay for bills that exceed normal usage only when the renter reported the problem promptly, the renter didn't cause the fault, and the service provider is not responsible.

heading: Appliance efficiency and moving out
text: Rental providers must replace appliances that do not meet efficiency requirements and pay the extra utility costs until they are replaced. When renters move out they must tell utility companies the date they are leaving; rental providers pay the costs between the renter leaving and the next renter moving in.
